subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes notices dark, velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of the skin in both axillae and on the posterior neck. The changes are symmetric and slowly progressive.
question: Which of the following best describes this finding and its clinical associations?

options.text: Painful raised subcutaneous nodules on the anterior shins associated with sarcoidosis
Diffuse fish-scale-like scaling associated with filaggrin gene mutations
Epidermal hyperplasia causing symmetric hyperpigmented thickening, associated with insulin resistance and visceral malignancy
Pruritic purple polygonal papules with white reticular mucosal lines, associated with hepatitis C
A herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree distribution of scaly plaques

explanation_correct: Acanthosis nigricans is epidermal hyperplasia producing symmetric, hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of the skin, especially in the axilla and neck. It is strongly associated with insulin resistance from diabetes, obesity, Cushing syndrome, or PCOS. It can also be a marker of visceral malignancy, particularly gastric adenocarcinoma. The symmetric hyperpigmented plaques in this diabetic patient are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Painful nodules on the anterior shins describe erythema nodosum, a panniculitis, not epidermal hyperplasia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Diffuse scaling with filaggrin mutations describes ichthyosis vulgaris, not hyperpigmented velvety thickening.
explanation_incorrect.D: Purple polygonal papules with Wickham striae and hepatitis C association describe lichen planus.
explanation_incorrect.E: A herald patch with a Christmas-tree distribution describes pityriasis rosea.

educationalObjective: Acanthosis nigricans is symmetric hyperpigmented epidermal hyperplasia in flexures, linked to insulin resistance and visceral malignancy such as gastric adenocarcinoma.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Miscellaneous skin disorders

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 27-year-old woman develops tender, raised erythematous nodules over both anterior shins. She recently had a sore throat and has a dry cough with hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiograph.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Erythema nodosum
Ichthyosis vulgaris
Lichen planus
Pityriasis rosea
Acanthosis nigricans

explanation_correct: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis causing painful, raised inflammatory nodules of subcutaneous fat, usually on the anterior shins. It is often idiopathic but is associated with sarcoidosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, streptococcal infections, leprosy, and inflammatory bowel disease. This patient's recent strep throat and hilar lymphadenopathy suggest both streptococcal infection and sarcoidosis as triggers.

explanation_incorrect.B: Ichthyosis vulgaris causes diffuse scaling from filaggrin mutations, not tender shin nodules.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lichen planus causes pruritic purple polygonal papules and Wickham striae, not painful subcutaneous nodules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch followed by scaly plaques in a Christmas-tree pattern, not tender nodules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acanthosis nigricans causes hyperpigmented velvety thickening in flexures, not painful shin nodules.

educationalObjective: Erythema nodosum is a painful panniculitis of the anterior shins associated with sarcoidosis, streptococcal infection, and other systemic conditions.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 5-year-old with a strong personal and family history of atopic dermatitis has had diffuse dry scaling of the skin since infancy, most pronounced on the extensor surfaces of the extremities and the trunk.
question: Which of the following best explains the underlying defect in this condition?

options.text: Autoantibodies against desmoglein in desmosomes
Excessive UV-induced apoptosis of keratinocytes
Post-radiation fibrosis with homogenized dermal collagen
IgA deposition at the tips of dermal papillae
Filaggrin gene mutation causing defective keratinocyte desquamation

explanation_correct: Ichthyosis vulgaris results from filaggrin gene mutations that disrupt keratinocyte desquamation, producing diffuse scaling of the skin. It most commonly affects the extensor surfaces of the extremities and the trunk and manifests in infancy or early childhood. There is a strong association with atopic dermatitis, as in this child. The other options describe autoimmune blistering, sunburn, radiation dermatitis, and dermatitis herpetiformis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anti-desmoglein autoantibodies cause pemphigus vulgaris, not a congenital scaling disorder.
explanation_incorrect.B: UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis underlies sunburn, not ichthyosis vulgaris.
explanation_incorrect.C: Homogenized dermal collagen after radiotherapy describes late radiation dermatitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: IgA at dermal papillary tips describes dermatitis herpetiformis, not ichthyosis vulgaris.

educationalObjective: Ichthyosis vulgaris is a filaggrin-mutation disorder of defective desquamation causing diffuse scaling in infancy, strongly associated with atopy.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 46-year-old has intensely pruritic, purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules and plaques on the wrists and shins. White reticular lines are noted on the oral mucosa. Biopsy shows hypergranulosis and a sawtooth lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction.
question: Which of the following systemic associations is classically linked to this condition?

options.text: Celiac disease
Hepatitis C infection
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Gastric adenocarcinoma
Sarcoidosis

explanation_correct: This is lichen planus, defined by the 6 P's: pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques. Mucosal involvement appears as Wickham striae, which are reticular white lines, and histology shows hypergranulosis with a sawtooth band of lymphocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction. Lichen planus is classically associated with hepatitis C infection. The other associations belong to different skin disorders.

explanation_incorrect.A: Celiac disease is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis, not lichen planus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is associated with erythema multiforme.
explanation_incorrect.D: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with acanthosis nigricans.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sarcoidosis is associated with erythema nodosum.

educationalObjective: Lichen planus shows the 6 P's, Wickham striae, and a sawtooth lymphocytic infiltrate and is associated with hepatitis C.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 23-year-old notices a single large, scaly erythematous patch on her trunk. Several days later she develops multiple smaller pink plaques with fine collarette scale arranged along skin lines in a Christmas-tree distribution over the trunk. The lesions resolve spontaneously after about 7 weeks.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Erythema nodosum
Lichen planus
Ichthyosis vulgaris
Pityriasis rosea
Erythema multiforme

explanation_correct: Pityriasis rosea begins with a single herald patch followed days later by multiple scaly erythematous plaques, often in a Christmas-tree distribution on the trunk. The plaques are pink with a collarette scale. The condition is self-resolving within 6-8 weeks, matching this patient's 7-week course. The other options have distinct morphologies and distributions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Erythema nodosum causes painful nodules on the anterior shins, not a herald patch and scaly plaques.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lichen planus causes pruritic purple polygonal papules with Wickham striae, not a Christmas-tree rash.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ichthyosis vulgaris causes chronic diffuse scaling from infancy, not an acute self-limited eruption.
explanation_incorrect.E: Erythema multiforme features target lesions with dusky centers, often after HSV or Mycoplasma infection.

educationalObjective: Pityriasis rosea features a herald patch then collarette-scaled plaques in a Christmas-tree distribution that self-resolve in 6-8 weeks.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old develops painful, bright red skin with dry, blanching erythema and small blisters after a full day in the sun, while a friend tans without burning. He recalls that the burning rays are different from the tanning rays.
question: Which of the following best explains the difference between sunburn and tanning ultraviolet radiation?

options.text: UVB predominates in tanning and photoaging, whereas UVA predominates in sunburn
UVA causes keratinocyte apoptosis, whereas UVB causes no DNA damage
UVB is dominant in sunburn, whereas UVA is dominant in tanning and photoaging; both UVA and UVB exposure increase skin cancer risk
UVA is completely absorbed by the ozone layer, so only UVB reaches the skin
Sunburn results from IgA-mediated inflammation of dermal papillae rather than keratinocyte apoptosis

explanation_correct: Sunburn is an acute cutaneous inflammatory reaction to excessive UV irradiation that induces DNA mutations and apoptosis of keratinocytes. UVB is the dominant wavelength in sunburn, whereas UVA predominates in tanning and photoaging. Exposure to both UVA and UVB increases the risk of skin cancer. This explains why one person burns while another tans.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses the roles: UVB dominates sunburn and UVA dominates tanning and photoaging.
explanation_incorrect.B: Both UVA and UVB can damage DNA; UVB is the dominant sunburn wavelength, and it is not true that UVB causes no damage.
explanation_incorrect.D: UVA does reach the skin; it penetrates deeply and is responsible for tanning and photoaging.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sunburn is due to UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis, not IgA deposition at dermal papillae (which occurs in dermatitis herpetiformis).

educationalObjective: UVB causes sunburn while UVA causes tanning and photoaging, and exposure to both raises skin cancer risk.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Miscellaneous skin disorders

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 62-year-old develops erythema and dry desquamation of the irradiated skin 3 weeks after radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, progressing to superficial ulceration and blistering. A different patient develops similar skin changes 2 years after radiation, with telangiectasias and biopsy showing homogenized dermal collagen fibers.
question: Which of the following best distinguishes acute from late radiation dermatitis?

options.text: Acute (90 days or less) results from basal keratinocyte apoptosis and epidermal edema, whereas late (months to years) results from fibrosis with homogenized dermal collagen and vascular damage
Acute disease is due to IgA at dermal papillary tips, whereas late disease is due to IgG against desmoglein
Both forms are caused by UVB-induced thymine dimers in keratinocytes
Acute disease shows a sawtooth lymphocytic infiltrate, whereas late disease shows neutrophilic panniculitis
Acute changes are type II hypersensitivity, whereas late changes are IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation

explanation_correct: Acute radiation dermatitis occurs within 90 days of radiotherapy and reflects apoptosis of basal keratinocytes and epidermal edema, producing erythema, desquamation, superficial ulceration, and blistering. Late radiation dermatitis appears months to years later and is due to fibrosis with homogenization of dermal collagen fibers, vascular damage, and telangiectasias. The 3-week presentation is acute, while the 2-year presentation with telangiectasias and homogenized collagen is late.

explanation_incorrect.B: IgA at dermal papillary tips describes dermatitis herpetiformis and anti-desmoglein IgG describes pemphigus vulgaris, not radiation injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: UVB-induced thymine dimers cause sunburn, not radiation dermatitis from therapeutic irradiation.
explanation_incorrect.D: A sawtooth lymphocytic infiltrate is lichen planus and neutrophilic panniculitis is not the mechanism of late radiation fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Radiation dermatitis is not a type II hypersensitivity or IgE-mediated process; it is direct radiation-induced tissue injury.

educationalObjective: Acute radiation dermatitis (90 days or less) is basal keratinocyte apoptosis with edema; late disease (months to years) is fibrosis with homogenized dermal collagen and telangiectasias.
